intro: A chronological library of free English texts from the earliest Christian centuries onward. Links open on other sites. Category key: New Testament (link only); Saint / Church Father; Other early Christian; Disputed / noncanonical; Non-Christian witness. A "Read with care" tag marks the few writings with a caution worth knowing; tap it to see why.

groups.title: AD 30–70 · Earliest years
questions: What happened after Jesus' death?
How did the apostles organize communities?
Where, how often, and how did Christians gather and worship?
How does the Eucharist relate historically to the Last Supper?
What did Peter, James, John, Paul and others do?
What happened as the apostles died?
groups.note: Surviving narrative and letters for this generation are almost entirely canonical New Testament texts. External notices are brief and later copied. Silence is not evidence.

evidence.shows: New Testament texts that Christians preserved as scripture describe early Jerusalem and diaspora communities, a shared meal tradition, and named leaders; Josephus mentions James; Roman historians mention Christians in connection with Rome under Nero and Claudius.
evidence.infer: Frequency of gatherings, exact local variety of meal practice, and day-to-day organization beyond what the texts happen to mention.
evidence.unknown: The full sequence of events after many apostles' deaths; most local community records; nearly all liturgical detail outside a few New Testament passages.

meanwhile.text: Rome under Hadrian; Hadrian’s Wall begun in Britain in the 122s — the wall from so many UK school trips.
Egypt: decades after Cleopatra’s death (30 BCE), Egypt is a Roman province — the movie Cleopatra era is already over.
Rome: Claudius is emperor; Rome invades Britain in 43 (the start of Roman Britain).
China: Eastern (Later) Han dynasty rules from Luoyang — a global anchor far from the Mediterranean.
Rome: Nero is emperor — the villain of countless movies and novels about Rome.
Britain: Boudica (Boudicca) leads the Iceni revolt against Rome — Warrior Queen territory.
Rome: Great Fire of Rome under Nero (the “fiddled while Rome burned” story is later legend).
Judaea: First Jewish Revolt; Titus takes Jerusalem and destroys the Second Temple in 70.
Mexico: Teotihuacán growing into a major city — pyramids rising while Nero rules Rome.

groups.title: AD 70–150 · After the apostles
questions: How was apostolic teaching transmitted?
Who led afterward?
What about bishops, presbyters, and deacons?
What did ordinary Christian life, prayer, baptism, and Sunday worship look like?
How did churches communicate and stay united?
What did Christians believe before the later councils?
groups.note: This is the densest surviving Christian letter-and-manual layer after the New Testament. Many texts traditionally linked to the apostles belong here.

evidence.shows: Letters from Rome, Antioch, and Smyrna; a church-order manual (Didache); an early martyr narrative for Polycarp; Pliny's provincial procedure under Trajan.
evidence.infer: How universal any one local pattern was; exact authorship of anonymous works.
evidence.unknown: Most local archives; full biographies of most leaders; whether some manuals describe ideal or actual practice.

meanwhile.text: These are Trajan’s own letters with Pliny — same emperor who pushed Rome to its widest east.
Judaea: Titus takes Jerusalem; Second Temple destroyed.
Italy: Mount Vesuvius erupts — Pompeii and Herculaneum buried (the disaster in every volcano documentary).
Rome: Colosseum inaugurated with games — gladiators for real, not just in movies.
Rome: Trajan emperor; the empire reaches its widest eastern extent.
China: Cai Lun reports improved papermaking to the Eastern Han court.
Rome: Hadrian; Hadrian’s Wall begun in Britain (122s) — still walkable today.
China: Eastern Han continues; Luoyang among the world’s largest cities.
Mexico: Teotihuacán rising — pyramids of the Sun and Moon taking shape.

groups.title: AD 150–325 · Developing Church
questions: How did the Mass and the sacraments take shape?
How was doctrine becoming defined?
What controversies arose?
What effects did persecution have?
What was the role of Rome and other churches?
How were authoritative writings determined?
groups.note: From Justin's ritual descriptions through Irenaeus and the African and Latin writers to Eusebius and Nicaea, this period has the richest primary documentation for worship, conflict, and canon.

evidence.shows: Second-century apologies and church manuals; named controversies (Marcion, Gnostic teachers, Quartodeciman Pascha dispute, rebaptism); martyr acts; third-century unity and baptism debates; early fourth-century imperial shift in Lactantius and Eusebius; Nicaea creed and canons.
evidence.infer: How typical any one city's liturgy was; motives in polemical sources.
evidence.unknown: Full texts of many opponents (often known only through critics); exact authorship of some church orders.

meanwhile.text: Constantine sole emperor after 324; Aksum a Red Sea power; Sasanian Persia.
Rome: Marcus Aurelius emperor — the philosopher-emperor; his son Commodus is the villain of the film Gladiator.
China–Rome contact: a reported envoy from Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court.
China: Han dynasty ends; Three Kingdoms period begins (220–265) — the era of countless East Asian novels and games.
Persia: Ardashīr I founds the Sasanian empire, ending Parthian rule.
Rome: Crisis of the Third Century — emperors rise and fall in rapid succession.
Mexico: Teotihuacán a major urban centre (Temple of Quetzalcóatl graves ~200 CE).
Africa: Kingdom of Aksum rising as a Red Sea trading power.
Rome: Edict of Milan — Constantine and Licinius grant toleration for Christianity.
Nicaea: First Council of Nicaea under Constantine.

groups.title: AD 325–1000 · After Constantine
questions: What changed after Constantine?
How did buildings, liturgy, vestments, art, and music develop?
Which councils clarified teaching?
How did monasticism grow?
How did East and West diverge?
Which early practices survived or changed?
groups.note: Selective coverage. Favor documents that show practice (Egeria, Cyril's mystagogical lectures, Apostolic Constitutions 8, monastic rules) and the great Christological and creedal councils, plus II Nicaea on images.

evidence.shows: Imperial patronage narratives; catechetical and liturgical descriptions; monastic rules; conciliar definitions; pilgrim observation of Jerusalem rites.
evidence.infer: How quickly local rites converged; how representative one pilgrim or one rule was.
evidence.unknown: Continuous musical notation for earliest chant; many ceremonial details before later Ordines.

meanwhile.text: Maya Classic cities (Palenque’s era approaching); late Gupta; Western Empire fading.

items.title: Commonitory
items.author: St. Vincent of Lérins
items.line: Treatise on the criterion of antiquity, universality, and consent. New Advent: NPNF translation.

meanwhile.text: Late Western Empire; Maya Classic; late Gupta India.

items.title: Tome (Letter 28)
items.author: Pope St. Leo the Great
items.line: Christological letter later received at Chalcedon. New Advent: NPNF translation.

meanwhile.text: Attila’s era — Catalaunian Plains is two years away (451); Maya Classic; Gupta ending.

items.title: Council of Chalcedon
items.author: Council of Chalcedon
items.line: Definition of faith and council acts. New Advent: council page.

meanwhile.text: Same year Romans and Visigoths check Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.

items.title: Rule of St. Benedict
items.author: St. Benedict of Nursia
items.line: Western monastic rule. Project Gutenberg landing for "St. Benedict's Rule for Monasteries."

meanwhile.text: Justinian reigning (527–565); later Arthurian legends are set around this post-Roman British age — legend, not history.

items.title: Pastoral Rule
items.author: Pope St. Gregory the Great
items.line: Handbook on the bishop as pastor. New Advent index to the books (NPNF).

meanwhile.text: Decades before the Hijrah (622); Tang China about to rise (618); Maya Classic continuing.

items.title: Second Council of Nicaea
items.author: Council of Nicaea II
items.line: Decree on images after the iconoclast controversy. New Advent: council page.

meanwhile.text: Six years before Vikings raid Lindisfarne (793); Charlemagne already king of the Franks (from 768); Tang China.
India: Gupta dynasty — a classical age of literature, math, and art.
Mesoamerica: Maya Classic Period — Tikal, Palenque, Copán (the cities in every Maya documentary).
Gaul: Attila checked at the Catalaunian Plains the same year as Chalcedon — the Hun from every barbarian epic.
West: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus — conventional end of the Western Roman Empire.
Britain: later Arthurian legends are set in this post-Roman age — legend, not verified history.
Byzantium: Justinian I; Hagia Sophia built.
China: Tang dynasty — often called a golden age of Chinese culture.
England: Vikings raid Lindisfarne — the attack that opens every Viking Age story.
Europe: Charlemagne crowned emperor of the Romans (800); dies 814.
Arabia: Hijrah — Muhammad migrates from Mecca to Medina; start of the Muslim era.

groups.title: AD 1000–present · Medieval Church onward
questions: How did the Mass reach recognizable forms?
How did spirituality, theology, and devotion develop?
Which modern Catholic traditions trace early, and which arose later?
groups.note: Selective milestones: a short spine of Mass and doctrine documents alongside spiritual classics. These establish official teaching at dated moments; they do not by themselves prove day-to-day parish practice.

evidence.shows: Official teaching and rubrical policy at dated moments (councils, papal constitutions, spiritual classics).
evidence.infer: Continuity claims with the earliest centuries are historical judgments, not automatic from the texts.
evidence.unknown: How every parish practiced day to day between these milestones.

items.title: Fourth Lateran Council — Canons
items.author: Fourth Lateran Council
items.line: Medieval council canons, including annual confession and communion discipline. Full council text on papalencyclicals.net.

meanwhile.text: Same year Magna Carta is sealed; Genghis Khan’s Mongols already reshaping Asia; Cahokia still a major Mississippian city.

items.title: Summa Theologiae
items.author: St. Thomas Aquinas
items.line: Theological work in three parts. New Advent: second and revised edition, 1920, tr. Fathers of the English Dominican Province. Primary link is an index.

meanwhile.text: Kublai Khan’s Mongol/Yuan era in Asia; Marco Polo will set out for China in 1271; Cahokia still occupied.

items.title: The Dialogue
items.author: St. Catherine of Siena
items.line: Written 1377–78. Tr. Algar Thorold, 1907 (CCEL work page leading to the text).

meanwhile.text: Decades after Mansa Musa’s famous hajj (1324); early Ming China (from 1368); Robin Hood ballads already circulating — legend, not a verified person.

items.title: The Imitation of Christ
items.author: Thomas à Kempis
items.line: Devotional work in four books, traditionally attributed to Thomas à Kempis. Tr. William Benham (Project Gutenberg).

meanwhile.text: Joan of Arc’s lifetime (c. 1412–1431) overlaps this window; Ming China; Aztec Tenochtitlán already founded (c. 1325).

items.title: Council of Trent — Session 13
items.author: Council of Trent
items.line: Decree on the Eucharist. English on papalencyclicals.net.

meanwhile.text: A generation after Henry VIII’s reign (d. 1547) and the Aztec and Inca conquests; young Teresa of Ávila already alive (b. 1515).

items.title: Council of Trent — Session 22
items.author: Council of Trent
items.line: Decree on the Sacrifice of the Mass. English on papalencyclicals.net.

meanwhile.text: Early Elizabeth I (from 1558); Teresa opens St. Joseph’s the same year; Ming China.

items.title: Life
items.author: St. Teresa of Ávila
items.line: Autobiography, 1565. Tr. David Lewis (Project Gutenberg).

links.label: Read at Project Gutenberg
links.expect: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus

meanwhile.text: Elizabeth I on the throne; Shakespeare baptized and Galileo born the year before (1564).

items.title: Quo Primum
items.author: Pope St. Pius V
items.line: Apostolic constitution on the Roman Missal. English on papalencyclicals.net.

meanwhile.text: Alive: Elizabeth I; Teresa of Ávila; young Shakespeare and Galileo (both b. 1564).

items.title: Interior Castle
items.author: St. Teresa of Ávila
items.line: Written 1577. Tr. Benedictines of Stanbrook, 1921 (CCEL).

meanwhile.text: Elizabeth I reigning; Shakespeare ~13; Galileo ~13; Philip II’s Spain.

items.title: Ascent of Mount Carmel
items.author: St. John of the Cross
items.line: Treatise on the spiritual life, c. 1580s. CCEL edition (public-domain translation).

meanwhile.text: Elizabeth I; Shakespeare; Galileo; Spanish Armada year 1588 falls in this decade.

items.title: Dark Night of the Soul
items.author: St. John of the Cross
items.line: Treatise on the spiritual life, c. 1580s. CCEL edition (public-domain translation).

meanwhile.text: Elizabeth I; Shakespeare; Galileo; same decade as the Armada (1588).

items.title: Introduction to the Devout Life
items.author: St. Francis de Sales
items.line: Book of spiritual instruction for lay people, 1609 (CCEL edition).

meanwhile.text: Jamestown founded two years earlier (1607); Pocahontas era; Galileo’s telescope work ~1609–10; Shakespeare still alive (d. 1616).

items.title: Story of a Soul
items.author: St. Thérèse of Lisieux
items.line: Autobiography, written 1895–97. Tr. T.N. Taylor, 1912 (Project Gutenberg).

meanwhile.text: Baseball is already America’s pastime (the Abner Doubleday 1839 invention story is legend); Culloden (1746) and the American Revolution sit in the long gap before this book.

items.title: Sacrosanctum Concilium
items.author: Second Vatican Council
items.line: Vatican II constitution on the sacred liturgy. Official English on vatican.va.

meanwhile.text: Cold War world; John F. Kennedy assassinated Nov 1963; Vatican II in session (1962–65).
England: William of Normandy wins at Hastings; from his line (via Matilda → Henry II) every later English/British monarch descends — including Charles III.

North America: Cahokia (near today’s St. Louis) flourishes — up to ~20,000 people; largest city north of Mexico before Europeans. (Pre-contact Cherokee politics are mostly unknown from written sources.)
Asia: Genghis Khan builds the Mongol empire — the conqueror from every world-history classroom.
West Africa: Mansa Musa’s gold-laden pilgrimage to Mecca makes Mali famous across the Mediterranean.
France: Joan of Arc leads French forces, then is executed (1431) — the Maid of Orléans of stage and screen.
Germany: Gutenberg completes his 42-line Bible — movable type that changes Europe.
Atlantic & Mexico: Columbus reaches the Caribbean (1492); Cortés and allies take Tenochtitlán (1521), ending Aztec imperial rule.
England: Henry VIII reigns — and his six wives become schoolroom legend.
England: Elizabeth I; Shakespeare baptized 1564 and Galileo born 1564 — the Tudor/Armada world of film and novels.
Virginia: Jamestown founded 1607; Pocahontas era. Scotland: Culloden 1746 ends the Jacobite rising (Outlander territory) — between Devout Life and Story of a Soul.

fun_overlaps.title: 1066 still sits on today’s British throne
fun_overlaps.detail: William wins at Hastings (1066). From his granddaughter Matilda’s son Henry II onward, every English (then British) monarch descends from William — including Charles III.

fun_overlaps.title: Teresa of Ávila and Elizabeth I
fun_overlaps.detail: Teresa’s Life (1565) and Interior Castle (1577) fall squarely in Elizabeth I’s reign (1558–1603) — rival Catholic and Protestant worlds, same decades.

fun_overlaps.title: Shakespeare and Galileo, born the year before Teresa’s Life
fun_overlaps.detail: Shakespeare baptized 1564; Galileo born 1564 — the year before Teresa’s Life (1565). Both alive through Quo Primum, Interior Castle, and John of the Cross’s 1580s works.

fun_overlaps.title: Devout Life while Jamestown and Pocahontas’s world open
fun_overlaps.detail: Francis de Sales’s Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) lands two years after Jamestown (1607), in the Pocahontas era — and the same years Galileo is turning his telescope on the sky.

fun_overlaps.title: Lateran IV and Magna Carta — same year
fun_overlaps.detail: Fourth Lateran Council canons and Magna Carta are both dated 1215.

fun_overlaps.title: Chalcedon and Attila — same year
fun_overlaps.detail: Council of Chalcedon (451) is the same year a Roman–Visigoth force checked Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.

fun_overlaps.title: Pompeii dies, Colosseum opens — within a year
fun_overlaps.detail: Vesuvius buries Pompeii in 79; Titus inaugurates the Colosseum with games in 80 — both just after the apostles’ generation.

fun_overlaps.title: Joan of Arc’s lifetime overlaps The Imitation of Christ
fun_overlaps.detail: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) is alive across the window usually given for The Imitation of Christ (c. 1418–27).

fun_overlaps.title: Cahokia a mega-city while Aquinas writes the Summa
fun_overlaps.detail: Cahokia near today’s St. Louis flourished c. 950–1350 (up to ~20,000 people) — still a major centre when Aquinas wrote the Summa (1265–74) and when Lateran IV met (1215).

fun_overlaps.title: Mansa Musa’s gold hajj before Catherine of Siena
fun_overlaps.detail: Mansa Musa’s spectacular pilgrimage (1324) is only about fifty years before Catherine’s Dialogue (1377–78).

fun_overlaps.title: Augustine writing while Maya Classic cities rose
fun_overlaps.detail: Confessions (c. 397–400) and City of God (413–426) overlap the Maya Classic Period (c. 250–900), when Tikal and other cities flourished.

fun_overlaps.title: Thérèse’s 1890s — baseball already America’s pastime
fun_overlaps.detail: By Story of a Soul (1895–97), baseball was established in the U.S. The Abner Doubleday “invented it in 1839” story is legend, not history.

fun_overlaps.title: Culloden (Outlander) sits between two Deep Dive books
fun_overlaps.detail: No Deep Dive writing is from 1746, but Culloden — the last Jacobite battle — falls in the long gap between Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) and Story of a Soul (1895–97).

fun_overlaps.title: Cai Lun’s paper and Ignatius/Trajan
fun_overlaps.detail: Around Ignatius’s letters (c. 107–110) and Pliny–Trajan (c. 112), Cai Lun was at the Eastern Han court; he reported improved papermaking c. 105.

fun_overlaps.title: Benedict’s Rule and the Arthur legend-setting
fun_overlaps.detail: Benedict’s Rule (c. 530) falls in the post-Roman British centuries where later Arthurian legends are set — Arthur himself is legend, not verified history.
